memoryText: Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen!
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Psalm 72:19 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse ends the second book of the Psalms with a burst of praise. It follows the long prayer for the king and carries the hope of the whole psalm into a doxology.

“Blessed be his glorious name forever.” To bless the name of God is to speak well of him, to honor him as he deserves. His name is his character and reputation, everything about him that has been revealed. The word “forever” is the language of eternity: not for a moment, not for a lifetime, but without end.

“May the whole earth be filled with his glory!” This is one of the Bible’s great prayers. It echoes Numbers 14:21, where God says, “All the earth shall be filled with the glory of the LORD.” It anticipates Habakkuk 2:14. It is the purpose of creation and redemption: that the glory of God would cover the earth as the waters cover the sea.

“Amen and Amen!” The double Amen is an emphatic “Let it be so.” It is the people’s agreement. They are not spectators but participants.

The context matters. This psalm is a prayer for a king, and the verse puts the king’s reign in its place. The king’s task is not to build his own name but to serve a purpose bigger than himself: the glory of God in all the earth. Solomon did not achieve this. His kingdom faded, and his temple fell. But the prayer remained, and it points to a king who will.

For the Christian, this is a prayer for the coming of Christ’s kingdom. When we pray “Hallowed be your name, your kingdom come,” we pray the same thing. And we live for it: that the earth would be filled with his glory. Let this be the prayer of your heart.
weekInReview: This week the Davidic story reached its end and the Solomonic age began. You read David’s last words and his oracle of the just king, and the sobering account of the census and the plague, which ended at the threshing floor that would become the temple mount. You saw Solomon anointed and David’s charge to him, and you watched Solomon ask for wisdom and show it. You read of the building of the temple, a miniature Eden where God would dwell. In the Psalms, you read the royal wedding song of Psalm 45, which Hebrews applies to the Son, and Psalm 72, the prayer for the king that no human king could answer. The week taught that David’s hope rested on an everlasting covenant, that wisdom is a gift from God, and that the temple, though glorious, pointed to a greater dwelling.
reflectionQuestions: David refused to offer God what cost him nothing. What does faithful worship cost you, and what are you tempted to hold back?
Hebrews says Psalm 45 is addressed to the Son: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.” How does it change your view of Jesus to hear him addressed this way?
Solomon asked for wisdom, and God gave him more. Where do you need wisdom this week, and how will you ask for it?
prayerPrompts: Bless God’s glorious name and pray for the earth to be filled with his glory.
Thank him for the King who judges with righteousness.
